title: About 880 NOAA Employees Laid Off in February 2025
description_short: About 880 NOAA Employees Laid Off in February 2025
description_medium: BBC News reported that about 880 National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration employees, including weather forecasters, were laid off in February 2025. Before that round, NOAA had about 12,000 staff worldwide, including 6,773 scientists and engineers. The agency said it would continue providing forecasts, warnings, and other information for public safety. The BBC account does not support the original title’s claim that more than 2,000 climate and weather scientists were fired.
description_long: BBC News reported on February 28, 2025, that around 880 NOAA employees, including weather forecasters, had been terminated in a round of federal workforce cuts. The article said NOAA had roughly 12,000 employees worldwide before the layoffs, including 6,773 scientists and engineers, and quoted the agency saying it would continue providing forecasts, warnings, and other information as part of its public-safety mission. It also reported that climate scientist Zack Labe said he had been fired, and described how NOAA data supports private weather services and the National Hurricane Center. The linked account documents roughly 880 terminations in that round; it does not substantiate the original title’s claim that more than 2,000 climate and weather scientists were fired, or show that NOAA’s forecasts had already failed because of the cuts.
notes: Focused read of the linked BBC report supports approximately 880 NOAA layoffs in February 2025, agency staffing figures, and the agency’s statement that it would continue its public-safety services. The unsupported 2,000-plus claim and assertions of service failure were removed.

title: DOJ Seeks Dismissal of Eric Adams Charges, Citing Immigration Policy
description_short: DOJ Seeks Dismissal of Eric Adams Charges, Citing Immigration Policy
description_medium: In February 2025, the Justice Department directed prosecutors in New York to seek dismissal of the five-count corruption indictment against Mayor Eric Adams. CBS News reports that Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove cited Adams’s ability to assist the administration’s immigration enforcement, while the motion also cited election-related concerns and Adams’s ability to govern. Prosecutors alleged a quid pro quo; Bove and Adams rejected that characterization. A judge’s approval was still required when the motion was filed, so the charges had not yet been dismissed.
description_long: CBS News reported in February 2025 that Acting Deputy Attorney General Emil Bove directed federal prosecutors in New York to seek dismissal of the five-count indictment against Mayor Eric Adams. Bove’s directive cited Adams’s restricted ability to assist the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement and other public-safety work. The motion filed in court also cited appearances of impropriety, risks of interference with New York City’s 2025 elections, and Adams’s ability to govern. The article reports that Southern District of New York U.S. Attorney Danielle Sassoon resigned rather than file the motion. Sassoon alleged that Adams’s lawyers had offered immigration-policy cooperation in exchange for dismissal; Bove and Adams rejected the quid-pro-quo characterization. The motion said the dismissal would be without prejudice and required judicial approval. The article therefore documents a DOJ request and internal dispute, not a final court dismissal or finding that an exchange occurred.
subcategory: DOJ Motion to Dismiss Adams Indictment
organization_tags: U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York
notes: Focused read of the linked CBS report confirms the DOJ directive, Bove’s stated rationale, the filed motion, Sassoon’s resignation, and that judicial approval was pending. The motion was described as without prejudice; no later dismissal or judicial quid-pro-quo finding is asserted.

title: Trump Orders 60-Day Review and Termination of Federal DEI Programs
description_short: Trump Orders 60-Day Review and Termination of Federal DEI Programs
description_medium: President Trump’s January 20, 2025 executive order directs OMB, with assistance from the attorney general and OPM, to coordinate termination of federal DEI and DEIA mandates, programs, policies, and activities. Agency heads are directed to take specified actions within 60 days, including terminating covered offices, positions, plans, grants, contracts, and performance requirements to the maximum extent allowed by law, and reporting existing programs and spending to OMB. The order sets directives and a deadline; it does not establish that every program or military initiative ended immediately.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed the executive order “Ending Radical and Wasteful Government DEI Programs and Preferencing.” The order directs the Office of Management and Budget, assisted by the attorney general and the Office of Personnel Management, to coordinate the termination of federal DEI and DEIA mandates, policies, programs, preferences, and activities. It also directs OPM to review federal employment practices and training policies. Within 60 days, agency heads must, to the maximum extent allowed by law, terminate covered DEI/DEIA and environmental-justice offices and positions, equity action plans and programs, related grants and contracts, and DEI/DEIA performance requirements. They must also report existing positions, programs, budgets, contractors, and grantees to OMB. The order states the administration’s rationale and prescribes agency actions and reporting; it does not itself show that every listed program had already ended on January 20, or document separate military implementation.
notes: Focused read of the official White House order confirms the coordination directive, covered program types, 60-day agency actions, and reporting requirements. The entry now distinguishes the order’s requirements from completed implementation and does not claim an immediate military-wide shutdown.
